title: Chopper Crash Probe Widens as Operators Threaten to Ground Char Dham Flights
excerpt: Investigators are examining flights before and after the fatal October 30 sortie, a two-pilot rule takes effect November 2, and 11 operators say they may suspend services in protest.
body:
• Investigators probing the October 30 Joshimath helicopter crash are now examining the flights that operated before and after the fatal sortie, along with weather and flight sequence, The Indian Express reported.
  • From November 2, Char Dham charter helicopters must fly with two pilots, take prior approval from UCADA's Helicopter Operations Officer for every take-off and landing, and file a pilot report after every flight.
  • Eleven charter operators have threatened to suspend Char Dham services from November 2, telling the DGCA the two-pilot rule makes operations commercially unviable.
  • If you have a Char Dham helicopter booking on or after November 2, check its status with your operator before travelling — services may be disrupted.

The investigation into the October 30 helicopter crash near Joshimath has widened beyond the crashed aircraft. Investigators are examining the flights that took off before and after the fatal sortie, the sequence of flights, and the weather conditions at the time, The Indian Express reported in an exclusive on November 1. DGCA and Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) teams reached Joshimath on Saturday, October 31, spoke to local residents, and were to visit the accident site with UCADA officials to collect evidence.

The crash itself was covered when it happened: a Trans Bharat Aviation helicopter flying from Badrinath to Sahastradhara in Dehradun on October 30 lost contact near Joshimath and crashed into a hillside, killing all six on board — pilot Captain Himanshu and five passengers from Bengaluru. What is new is the regulatory response, the widened probe, and a standoff with operators that could ground Char Dham flights from Monday.

New Rules From November 2

At a high-level meeting on October 31 between the Uttarakhand Civil Aviation Development Authority (UCADA) and the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), officials decided that all Char Dham charter services will run with a "two-pilot crew configuration," UCADA Chief Executive Officer Prateek Jain told the media, in reporting carried by The Hindu.

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2116915819842035959

"The two-pilot crew will be mandatory from November 2."

— Prateek Jain, Chief Executive Officer, UCADA

Prior approval of UCADA's Helicopter Operations Officer will now be mandatory for each flight to take off and land. Pilots must also submit a report after every flight detailing weather conditions and other operational information; Jain said a standard format is being prepared, and the reports are intended to help pilots on subsequent flights evaluate conditions. According to sources cited in the same reporting, the two-pilot arrangement will not be available for helicopter services at Kedarnath, and a pilot over 60 can serve as co-pilot if qualified to operate in mountainous areas.

Operators Threaten to Stop Flying

Operators have pushed back. Eleven charter operators have threatened to suspend Char Dham services from November 2, in a joint representation to DGCA chief Vir Vikram Yadav, the Civil Aviation Ministry and the Uttarakhand government, Mirror Now reported.

The operators argue that a second pilot on every sortie raises crew salary, training, accommodation and logistics costs in ways that cannot be absorbed under current rates, and that passing the cost to passengers is not feasible. They say new safety measures must be proportionate and commercially sustainable, and have asked the DGCA and UCADA for urgent discussions and an alternative framework. As of November 1, the suspension remained a threat, not a confirmed shutdown.

What This Means for Pilgrims

Two things are now running in parallel: an AAIB-led investigation that has widened to the flights around the fatal one, and a November 2 deadline that could either bring in a stricter two-pilot regime or disrupt services if operators carry out their threat.

Anyone booked on a Char Dham helicopter service on or after November 2 should confirm the flight's status directly with the operator before setting out. No official cause for the October 30 crash has been established, and readers should treat early explanations — weather or otherwise — as unconfirmed until the investigation reports.
